name: Vera Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good to meet you, Vera. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not connected to any company, union, party or government, and your answers stay confidential. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a water cart at the Redgum bauxite mine. That's a big truck with a tank and sprayers, and I keep the haul roads wet so the dust stays down. I'm on a labour-hire contract, so technically I work for an agency, not the mine. Twelve hours, back and forth, refill at the standpipe, back and forth again.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it matters. If I don't water, the truck drivers can't see and somebody gets hurt. What wears me out is that nobody notices unless I miss a patch. And the contract gets renewed every three months, so I never quite relax.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about life outside work.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Tomas, he's a welder at a fabrication shop that does repairs for the mine. We're getting married in April at the church I grew up in. We're paying for most of it ourselves, so every spare dollar goes there. Savings, honestly, maybe two weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me read you the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. I'd be happy with that one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. People in cities get excited about every new gadget. Out here, work is still work. I'd say that after church, probably, to my uncle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, nothing changes, and that's still hard. My contract gets reviewed in February. The agency already told us the mine wants fewer contractors next year because of costs. That has nothing to do with AI. It's just money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down, never be late, never miss a patch. I'd ask the agency if I can get a direct job with the mine, which is safer. And I'd cut the wedding guest list a bit, even though Mum won't like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, honestly. The wedding, the contract in February, and Tomas's shop depends on the same mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Tomas's shop depends on the same mine. How much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of their work is mine repairs, maybe three quarters. If the bauxite mine cuts costs, my contract and my fiancé's welding work both go wrong at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut from the wedding first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The band. My cousin plays guitar, he'd do it for free. The dress stays, I've already paid half. The church is free for members anyway.

say: I'd say **city people** get excited about every new gadget.
I'd tell my uncle after church that **work is still work** out here.
think: My **contract review** in February worries me more than AI.
The mine wants **fewer contractors** next year because of costs.
do: Ask the agency about a **direct job** with the mine.
Cut the **wedding band** and some guests to save money.
feel: **Worried** about the wedding, the contract, and Tomas's shop all at once.
S0.quote: If the bauxite mine cuts costs, my contract and my fiancé's welding work both go wrong at once.
fieldNote: Vera's anxiety comes from a **three-month contract** and a February review, not AI.
Her household has **one point of failure**: both incomes depend on the same mine.
She speaks with **traditional** frames: city people, church, family paying for the wedding.

steps.text: Ask the labour-hire agency about a direct job at the bauxite mine
Replace the wedding band with her cousin on guitar
Turn up early every shift before the February contract review

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. I don't love the sound of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office people and the computer companies who wanted this, not us. I'd say working people should come first. I'd probably say it at the family lunch on Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think a water cart is one of the easiest jobs to give a robot. Same roads, same sprayers, over and over. If the mine plans the routes with AI, they don't need me to decide where to spray. I'm the first one they'd test it on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stick to my job and do it perfectly. I wouldn't do computer courses, that's not me. I'd ask my pastor if the church knows of other work in town, just in case. And Tomas and I would push the wedding savings harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like waiting for the contract email, but all the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're the first they'd test a robot on. Do you think they already are?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know for sure. Last month a man from head office rode in my water cart with a laptop, asking about the routes, and nobody told me why. I've thought about it every day since.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever consider learning the new systems?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a person showed me, in the truck, with my hands, maybe. Not on a phone, not with a chat thing. I don't trust it. My grandad learned everything by watching, and so did I.

say: I'd say **office people** and computer companies wanted this, not us.
I'd say **working people** should come first.
think: A **water cart** is one of the easiest jobs to give a robot.
If AI plans the routes, I'm the **first one** they'd test.
do: Do my job **perfectly** and skip computer courses.
Ask my **pastor** if the church knows other work in town.
feel: **Anxious**, like waiting for the contract email all the time.
S1.quote: A man from head office rode in my water cart with a laptop, asking about the routes, and nobody told me why.
fieldNote: Vera already sees **signs** of automation in her own cab and dwells on them.
She rejects **screen learning** but might accept hands-on teaching in the truck.
She turns to **church and family** networks rather than government help.

steps.text: Ask her pastor about other work in town
Keep every shift perfect and avoid any warnings
Put Tomas's overtime pay straight into wedding savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next one is much faster. It's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? No. Please, no.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is wrong, and people should stop it. I'd say it to anybody who listened, at church, at work. I'd say politicians who let this happen should be voted out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I don't have a plan. AGI in 2028 means the routes and the agency's rosters are done by a computer. Then by 2031 my truck drives itself. Tomas's shop loses work too. We'd be newly married with nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd postpone the wedding, honestly, or make it tiny. I'd move back in with my parents. I'd vote for whoever promised to protect jobs at the mine. Beyond that, I really don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked. I can feel my chest go tight just saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the wedding is off for now. She'd cry, because she's been planning it since I was little. Telling my mum the wedding is off is the part I can't picture saying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't have a plan. What would it take to make one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money and time, and I'd have neither. Maybe if the mine kept us on for a year while we figured it out. But I don't think they would.

say: I'd say this is **wrong** and people should stop it.
Politicians who allow it should be **voted out**.
think: By 2031 my **truck drives itself** and Tomas's shop loses work.
Tomas and I would be **newly married** with nothing to live on.
do: **Postpone the wedding** or make it tiny.
Vote for whoever promises to **protect mine jobs**.
feel: **Panicked**, with my chest going tight just saying it.
S2.quote: Telling my mum the wedding is off is the part I can't picture saying.
fieldNote: Vera has **no plan** and says so; she lacks both money and time.
The **wedding** becomes the first casualty and the most painful one.
Her response is **political**: vote out those who allow it.

steps.text: Postpone the April wedding or shrink it to family only
Move back in with her parents to save rent
Vote for candidates who promise to protect mine jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same idea, a bit slower. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it again: this should be stopped or slowed down. Five years is not long for a town like ours. I'd join any group at church or in town that was writing to the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means we'd be married, maybe with a baby. AGI in 2031, robots in 2034. I'd be 34 with a water cart licence and nothing else. That frightens me more than the two-year one in some ways, because there'd be a child.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go ahead with the wedding, but small. I'd ask the agency to train me on a different truck, something with more skill, if they would. Tomas might try to get work at a bigger fabrication shop in the city. We'd save harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It doesn't go away, it just takes longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Tomas might go to the city. Would you go with him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to stay near my parents and the church. But if that's where the work is, I'd go. A wife goes where the family needs to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you put off children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. That's a hard thing to say. I always wanted to be young when I had kids, like my mum was, and robots at the mine would make me wait.

I'd join a **church or town group** writing to the government.
think: At **34** I'd have a water cart licence and nothing else.
A **baby** would make this scarier than the two-year picture.
do: Have a **small wedding** and save harder.
Ask the agency to train me on a **more skilled truck**.
feel: **Alarmed**: the fear doesn't go away, it just takes longer.
S3.quote: I always wanted to be young when I had kids, like my mum was, and robots at the mine would make me wait.
fieldNote: The extra time brings **children** into Vera's thinking, which raises the stakes.
She'd follow **Tomas** to the city, despite wanting to stay near family and church.
She'd join a **community letter-writing** group rather than a union.

steps.text: Hold a small church wedding in April and save the rest
Ask the agency for training on a more skilled haul truck
Join a church group writing to the government about mine jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. It's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to protect people if leaders want to. I'd say communities like ours need support for apprenticeships and family businesses, not handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years plus three is 2039. I'd be 40. The mine might still need some people. I might be in a different job by then anyway. It's still worrying, but I could breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get married in April as planned. I'd ask the agency to put me on more skilled trucks over the next few years. Tomas and I might try to start a small repair business together, him welding, me doing the books, though I'd need help with the computer side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not scared out of my mind. More like a heavy thought in the back of my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd need help with the computer side. Who would help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomas's sister works at the bank. She'd show me. I'd learn it from a person, not from an app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your family say about you starting a business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad would be proud. Working for yourself is the best kind of work, my dad always said, and with ten years my fiancé Tomas and I could try it. Mum would worry about the money.

say: I'd say **ten years** is enough to protect people if leaders want to.
Communities need **apprenticeships** and family businesses, not handouts.
think: Robots by 2039 means I'd be **40**, maybe already in a different job.
It's **still worrying**, but I could breathe.
do: Start a small **repair business** with Tomas, him welding and me on the books.
feel: **Anxious**, like a heavy thought at the back of my head.
S4.quote: Working for yourself is the best kind of work, my dad always said, and with ten years my fiancé Tomas and I could try it.
fieldNote: The decade gives Vera room for a **family business**, which fits her values.
She'd learn computer bookkeeping only from **a person**, Tomas's sister.
Her worry stays **anxious** because her contract and savings are still thin.

steps.text: Get married in April as planned
Ask the agency for more skilled truck work over the next years
Start a small welding repair business with Tomas

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt. The wedding, the job, Tomas's shop, all gone at once. What would help is the mine keeping local people on while we retrain, and help for small family businesses to start up.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. A lot of people in our church would get through this together, sharing meals and lending money. That's what would keep me going, not an app.

headlineQuote: A lot of people in our church would get through this together, sharing meals and lending money.
portrait: Vera is a **water cart driver** on a three-month labour-hire contract at a bauxite mine.
She's engaged to Tomas, a welder whose shop also depends on **the same mine**.
She's already anxious about a **February contract review** before AI comes up.
She rejects **screen learning** and leans on church and family.
In the fast AGI picture she has **no plan** and would postpone her wedding.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her job, Tomas's shop and the wedding would all go at once.
whatWouldHelp: The mine **keeping local people** on while they retrain.
Help for **small family businesses** to start up.
